bars: On football, Strategy A with a good prompt beats Strategy B for four of five models. A best reaches F1 0.19–0.43 and B with memory 0.12–0.23. Only gpt-oss:120b, the most cautious model under Strategy A, scores as high with B + memory (0.20) as with its best prompt (0.19). Zero-shot is the weakest A condition for the cautious models (F1 0.06–0.10), and B beats it. For deepseek and mistral, even zero-shot A (0.37 and 0.29) is far above B. On F1 ign, A best (0.40–0.65) is above B + memory (0.43–0.51) for gemma4, mistral and deepseek, ties for gpt-oss:20b (0.43) and is below it for gpt-oss:120b (0.40 vs 0.48).
forest: The paired differences confirm this. Against A zero-shot, B + memory is significantly better for gpt-oss:20b (+0.08), gemma4 (+0.11) and gpt-oss:120b (+0.14), and significantly worse for deepseek (−0.25); for mistral the interval includes 0 (−0.06). Against A best, B + memory is significantly worse for gemma4 (−0.10), mistral (−0.18) and deepseek (−0.31), and not different for gpt-oss:20b and gpt-oss:120b. With abstentions ignored most intervals include 0; the clear exceptions are mistral, whose answers are less accurate with B + memory than with A best (−0.18), and gpt-oss:20b, whose answers are less accurate with B search than with A zero-shot (−0.25).
taskwise: Counting tasks, A best and B get different tasks right. For gpt-oss:120b, 22 tasks are right only with A best and 22 only with B + memory (p = 1.0). For the other models, A best wins clearly (40–87 tasks only A, 9–21 only B, all p ≤ 0.009). The overlap is small: 8–27 tasks are right under both, so the two strategies are partly complementary.
pr: In precision–recall space, A best lies to the right of B for every model except gpt-oss:120b: A answers far more tasks at similar or higher precision. B's precision on football (0.22–0.34) is below that of A zero-shot and A best for deepseek and mistral (0.37–0.49).
strata: Pooled over models, A best is ahead of B + memory in every stratum, with the largest gaps where A is strongest: low-G tasks (F1 0.41 vs 0.23) and mid-centrality nodes (0.39 vs 0.23). B is flat across strata (0.15–0.23). B gains nothing where the hidden property is common (high H: A best 0.34, B + memory 0.17), unlike on airports, where search helps most for popular properties.
identifiers: The name helps A much more than B. In the high-G tasks, A best goes from F1 0.20 to 0.45 and F1 ign 0.40 to 0.66 when the name is given; B + memory goes only from 0.13 to 0.22 and its F1 ign stays at 0.37–0.38. With the name, the model often recognises the player from its training data. B also finds the player's page, but then reads the wrong value from it.
difficulty: Both strategies score highest on the hardest tertile (A best 0.40, B + memory 0.24) and the gap between them is similar in every tertile (0.10–0.17 F1). The difficulty score does not separate the tasks where retrieval helps from those where it does not.
properties: Per property, B helps where a value is published in a standard place: *Goals conceded per 90 minutes* (F1 0.44 with B + memory vs 0.30 for A best) and *Name* (0.31 vs 0.00). It also gives a better F1 ign for *Losses* (0.50 vs 0.33) and *Wins* with memory (0.40 vs 0.20). A best is far ahead on values the model can estimate: *Minutes per start* (0.82 vs 0.42), *Date of birth* (0.79 vs 0.21), *Penalties missed* (0.61 vs 0.36) and *Assists* (0.48 vs 0.25). *Position* and *On-offsides* are almost never right under any approach.
complementarity: Because A best and B get different tasks right, combining them helps. A deployable rule, *use B and fall back on A when B abstains*, beats A best for gpt-oss:20b (F1 0.27 vs 0.25) and gpt-oss:120b (0.24 vs 0.19), ties for gemma4 (0.29) and loses for mistral (0.34 vs 0.41) and deepseek (0.39 vs 0.43), whose B answers are worse than their A answers. An oracle that picks whichever is right would reach 0.27–0.46. That bounds what a confidence-based selector could gain: 0.03–0.09 over A best.
same_answer: When both strategies answer, they agree on the value in only 9–19% of the tasks. Agreement is a useful confidence signal only for the strong models: for mistral, an answer both strategies give is right 64% of the time, against 48% (A) and 33% (B) when they differ. For the smaller models the agreed answers are no more reliable than the others, because they share the same wrong default values.
energy: B costs much more than A for a lower F1 on football. A run of B takes 0.36–1.69 Wh, 23–120× the energy of the same model's best A prompt (0.003–0.069 Wh). Its token amplification is 6.2–7.0×, against 1.1–3.9× for A. Every model's A points dominate its B points (higher or equal F1 at lower energy) except gpt-oss:120b, where B + memory gains 0.015 F1 for 38× the energy.
stability: The three runs of A best agree on the outcome for 60% of the tasks on average and those of A zero-shot for 83%. B is in between (search 71%, memory 67%). The A best prompt is often compact, which is the least stable prompt. Stability does not differ enough to change the comparison.
takeaways:
1. **On football, A with a good prompt beats B** for four of five models (A best F1 0.19–0.43 vs B + memory 0.12–0.23); only gpt-oss:120b ties (0.19 vs 0.20).
2. **B beats zero-shot A only for the cautious models** (gpt-oss:20b, gemma4, gpt-oss:120b: +0.08 to +0.14 F1), and mainly because it abstains less than they do under zero-shot.
3. **The two strategies are complementary**: few tasks are right under both, and *B, then A if B abstains* improves on A best for the two gpt-oss models; an oracle would add 0.03–0.09 F1.
4. **The player's name helps A (+0.25 F1) much more than B (+0.09)**: memory recognises the player; search finds the page but reads the wrong value.
5. **B is 23–120× more expensive** in energy than the model's best A prompt and amplifies the user's input 6–7×, for a lower F1 on this dataset.
